title: str()
summary: The text type, and the function that converts any object to its readable form.
description: Python strings are immutable sequences of Unicode code points. Every method that 'changes' a string returns a new one — `s.upper()` does not modify `s`.

parameters.name: object
parameters.description: Object to render as text, via its __str__.

examples.title: f-strings are the readable way to interpolate
examples.code:
name, n = 'Ada', 3
print(f'{name} has {n} items, {n / 7:.2f} each')

examples.title: input() always gives you str
examples.code:
value = '5'
print(value + 1 if False else int(value) + 1)

real_world_usage: Everywhere. Notably: building messages, formatting reports, and the boundary where external input arrives as text and must be converted.

common_mistakes.fix: Strings are immutable. Assign the result: s = s.upper().

common_mistakes.mistake: Building a big string with += in a loop
common_mistakes.fix: Each += copies the whole string, making the loop quadratic. Collect into a list and ''.join() once.
TypeError. Convert explicitly with int() — Python will not guess.

performance_notes: Concatenating in a loop with += is O(n^2); str.join is O(n) and is the idiom. Strings are interned and hashed once, which is what makes them good dict keys.
security_notes: Never build SQL, shell commands or HTML by string interpolation of untrusted values — use parameterised queries, argument lists, and a template engine that escapes.
